newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Televisa seen adopting team leadership.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Televisa seen adopting team leadership.

text.p: Now more than ever, the leadership at Mexico's Grupo Televisa SA will be a team game, analysts said on Thursday.

With the death Wednesday of its dynamic and all-powerful leader Emilio Azcarraga Milmo, Televisa will enter a new era, relying on an executive committee making group decisions rather than on the man known as "El Tigre," who built Televisa into the Spanish-speaking world's biggest media group.
Azcarraga died in Miami at the age of 66 from cancer.
Changes began in the group on March 3 when Azcarraga stepped down as chairman.

At that time he formally handed the reins over to his son, Emilio Azcarraga Jean, 29, now president and chief executive officer, and Guillermo Canedo White, now chairman of the board and chief corporate officer.

"The future of the administration will be much more balanced," Francisco Rivero, an analyst with Valores Finamex in New York, told Reuters in a telephone interview. "Even though there were other people near the top involved in decisions, in the end it was usually Emilio Azcarraga who made them."
"It will be very difficult for Televisa to return to the past way of doing things," he added.
Planned in conjunction with those changes is the naming of an executive committee to be made up of an as-yet-unknown number of company insiders and perhaps some outside personalities, analysts said.
Several chiefs of other big Mexican companies currrently sit on the Televisa board.
"With the namings (of Azcarraga Jean and Canedo White in March), the new administration is pretty much intact and there is continuity," said Martin Lara, an analyst with Caspian in Mexico City.
For that reason, Lara said, Televisa shares are not likely to suffer from Azcarraga Milmo's death.
"There could be a psychological impact, but only in the very short term," Lara said.
Televisa shares in Mexico were down fractionally, falling 30 centavos on Wednesday night's close in light trade to 103.70 pesos. In New York, the ADRs were off 1/8 to 26-3/8.

Analysts said they expected the new leadership to continue a cost-cutting campaign, but few dared to speculate whether Televisa would distance itself from the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which traditionally has counted on Televisa and Azcarraga as reliable allies at election time.
Mid-term elections in Mexico are set for July 6, and Azcarraga Jean indicated in an interview with the Mexican news magazine Proceso that he was more interested in ratings than politics.
Televisa shareholders are expected to approve the executive committee concept next Wednesday in a quarterly meeting.
Other names mentioned as candidates for the executive board are:
-- Miguel Aleman Velasco, a Mexican senator, Televisa's vice chairman and head of company's direct-to-home satellite television arm
-- Miguel Aleman Mangani, the former's son, vice president of the board and vice president for corporate communications
-- Jaime Davila, chief operating officer and the former chief of the Spanish-languague network Univision, regarded as the fifth-largest network in the United States.
Most of the attention is likely to focus on Azcarraga Jean, who takes over the family business at 29.
When his father inherited the reins from his grandfather, he was 42. Azcarraga Jean has yet to prove he has his father's business savvy.
Any charges at the top in Televisa are likely to seem radical, one Televisa expert said.

"Azcarraga was such a forceful personality, such a living legend, that not only has much of what Televisa done in the past 25 years been attributed to him, but it was difficult to get Televisa executives to acknowledge anything that wasn't his doing," Andrew Paxman, Variety's correspondent for Latin America, told Reuters.
"The question is how much talent is left behind," Paxman said. "Only time will tell."

Among the challenges the new team will face is the rising strength of the competition. Rival Mexican network Television Azteca still trails badly in market share, 74 percent to 26 percent, but grew steadily in 1996.
